Recall that a set $T\subset\mathbb{N}$ is \define{thick} if it contains arbitrarily long blocks of consecutive integers.
The properties of being thick and being syndetic are dual in the following sense: a set is thick if and only if it has nonempty intersection with every syndetic set, and vice versa.

\]

\[

\]
is less than the distance $d(U,U+\theta)/\theta$.

\[

\]

\]

Let  $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ with $\mathsf{d}^*(A)> 0$.  By combining the results in~\cite[Section~2]{MRR}, we can find  $\varepsilon > 0$, a F\o lner sequence $\Phi  = (\Phi_N)_{N\in\mathbb{N}}$, and a set $L\subset \mathbb{N}$ such that for every nonempty finite set $F\subset L$, the set
$$
\bigcap_{x\in F}(A-x)\cap\Big\{n\in\mathbb{N}\colon \mathsf{d}_\Phi\bigl((A-n)\cap L\bigr)> \varepsilon\Big\}
$$
has positive density with respect to $\Phi$. 
Let $F_1\subset F_2\subset \cdots\subset L$ be an exhaustion of $L$ by finite sets. 
For $i\in\mathbb{N}$, define
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:def-Qi}
Q_i = \bigcap_{x\in F_i}(A-x)\cap\Big\{n\in\mathbb{N}\colon \mathsf{d}_\Phi\bigl((A-n)\cap L\bigr) > \varepsilon\Big\}. 
\end{equation}
Pick $N(\mathcal{D}, \delta)\in\mathbb{N}$ such that for any interval $J\subset\mathbb{N}$ of length at least $N(\mathcal{D}, \delta)$ and any set $E\subset J$ with $|E|\geq \delta |J|$, there exists $X\in\mathcal{D}$ with $X\subset E$. 
Set $\delta_i = \mathsf{d}_\Phi(Q_i)/2$ and for each $i\in\mathbb{N}$, let $J_i\subset \mathbb{N}$ denote an interval whose length is at least $N(\mathcal{D}, \varepsilon\delta_i/2)$ and satisfies 
$$|J_i\cap Q_i|\geq \delta_i|J_i|.
$$
Without loss of generality, we can further assume that for each $i\in\mathbb{N}$, we have $\max J_i < \min J_{i+1}$.  
Then by~\eqref{eq:def-Qi}, it follows that 
\begin{enumerate}
\item \label{item:one}
$F_i+(Q_i\cap J_i)\subset A$ for all $i\in\mathbb{N}$.
\item 
If  $n_1< n_2< \cdots$ is an enumeration of $\bigcup_{i\in\mathbb{N}}(J_i\cap Q_i)$, then 
$$\mathsf{d}_\Phi\bigl((A-n_k)\cap L\bigr) > \varepsilon.$$
\end{enumerate}
Applying Bergelson's Intersectivity Lemma~\cite[Theorem~2.1]{bergelson}, there exists $K\subset\mathbb{N}$ with $\mathsf{d}(K) = \varepsilon$ such that for all nonempty finite sets $H\subset K$, we have 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:berg-cor}
\mathsf{d}^*\Bigl(\bigcap_{k\in H}\bigl((A-n_k)\cap L\bigr)\Bigr) > 0.
\end{equation}
Define
\[
R_i = \{n_k\colon k\in K\}\cap J_i\cap Q_i 
\]
and let $I\subset\mathbb{N}$ be an infinite set such that for all $i\in I$, we have 
\[
|R_i|\geq \frac{\varepsilon\delta_i}{2}|J_i|
\]
which exists because $\mathsf{d}(K) = \varepsilon$ and $|J_i\cap Q_i|\geq \delta_i|J_i|$. Since the length of $J_i$ exceeds $N(\mathcal{D}, \varepsilon\delta_i/2)$, we can find $X_i\in \mathcal{D}$ with $X_i\subset R_i$.
Then by property~\ref{item:one} and~\eqref{eq:berg-cor}, we conclude that 
\begin{enumerate}[resume]
\item
\label{item:three} 
$F_i+X_i\subset A$ for all $i\in I$. 
\item \label{item:four} 
For each $i\in I$, we have  
$$\mathsf{d}^*\Bigl(\bigcap_{x\in X_1\cup\ldots\cup X_i}\bigl((A-x)\cap L\bigr)\Bigr) > 0.
$$
\end{enumerate}
We are now ready to inductively construct the sets $B_1, B_2,\ldots$ and $C_1, C_2, \ldots$.  

First choose $B_1\in\mathcal{D}$ such that $B_1\subset L$. Choose $i_1\in I$ sufficiently large such that 
$B_1\subset F_{i_1}$, and  define $C_1 = X_{i_1}$.  By Property~\eqref{item:three}, we have that 
$$B_1+C_1\subset A.$$
Assume we have defined the sets $B_1, \ldots, B_n$ and $C_1, \ldots, C_n$ such that 
$B_1, \ldots, B_n\subset L$ and $C_1 = X_{i_1}, \ldots, C_n = X_{i_n}$ for some $i_1 < i_2 < \ldots <  i_n\in I$. 
Then by Property~\eqref{item:four}, there exists $B_{n+1}\in\mathcal{D}$ such that 
\[
B_{n+1}\subset\bigcap_{x\in X_{i_1}\cup\cdots\cup X_{i_n}}\bigl((A-x)\cap L\bigr).
\]
It follows that $B_{n+1}\subset L$ and for all $1\leq k \leq n$, we have 
\[
B_{n+1}+C_k\subset A. \]
Choose $i_{n+1}\in I$ that is sufficiently large such that  
\[
B_1\cup \cdots \cup B_n\cup B_{n+1}\subset F_{i_{n+1}}
\]
and set $C_{n+1} = X_{i_{n+1}}$.  
Then it follows from Property~\eqref{item:three} that 
for all $1 \leq k \leq n+1$, we have
$$B_k+C_{n+1}\subset A, 
$$
completing the proof.

    \forall F\in[m-1]^{<k},\ \forall\ell\leq k,\qquad p\not|\left(1+\ell x_p+\sum_{i\in F}b(i)\right).
\end{equation}
Note that there are at most $k2^{m-1}$ values of $x_p\bmod p$ that do \emph{not} satisfy~\eqref{eq_proof_BBtprimes5b}; therefore for each $p>k2^{m-1}$ we can choose a value of $x_p$ that does satisfy~\eqref{eq_proof_BBtprimes5b}.
Observe that this choice of $x_p$ satisfies~\eqref{eq_proof_BBtprimes4b} for all $n<m$ and $p<k2^{m}$.
Let $q=\prod_{p<k2^{m}}p$ and use the Chinese remainder theorem to find $a\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $a\equiv x_p\bmod p$ for every $p<k2^{m}$.
Next let
$$H:=\left\{1+\sum_{i\in F}b(i):F\in[m-1]^{<k}\right\}.$$
Note that $|H|\leq 2^{m-1}$.
It follows from~\eqref{eq_proof_BBtprimes3b} that for each $p<2^{m-1}\leq k2^{m-1}$, $|\{b(n)\bmod p:n\leq m-1\}|\leq1+\log_2(p/k)< p$ and hence that $H$ is an admissible set.
It follows from~\eqref{eq_proof_BBtprimes4b} that $(a+h,q)=1$ for every $h\in H$.

In view of \cref{lemma_DHLinprogressions}, there exists $b(m)>b(m-1)$ such that $b(m)+H\subset\mathbb{P}$ and $b(m)\equiv a\bmod q$.
From $b(m)+H\subset\mathbb{P}$ we deduce that~\eqref{eq_proof_BBtprimesb} holds with $n=m$.
From $b(m)\equiv a\bmod q$ and the fact that $a\equiv x_p\bmod p$ for every prime $p<k2^{m}$ we deduce that~\eqref{eq_proof_BBtprimes3b} holds with $n=m$.
Finally, from~\eqref{eq_proof_BBtprimes5b}, we deduce that~\eqref{eq_proof_BBtprimes4b} holds with $n=m$ for every prime $p<k2^{m}$.
